title: A brief review of portfolio optimization techniques
abstract_summary: This review surveys classical, statistical and intelligent approaches to portfolio optimization, covering methods from mean-variance and VaR/CVaR to machine learning, deep learning, reinforcement learning, evolutionary algorithms and quantum-inspired techniques. It discusses why portfolio optimization is important, the role of AI/ML in improving allocation decisions, and provides a comparative compilation of advantages, limitations and recent advances including quantum-inspired methods.
methodology_description: This paper is a narrative literature review (brief review) that surveys portfolio optimization techniques across classical, statistical and intelligent approaches and also compiles quantum-inspired and early quantum computing methods applicable to portfolio optimization. The authors organize the review by first describing portfolio types and risk/return measures (e.g. mean-variance, MAD, VaR, CVaR, LPM), then summarizing classical optimization methods, followed by intelligent approaches (Bayesian, SVM, neural networks, reinforcement learning, evolutionary algorithms) and finally quantum and quantum-inspired metaheuristics. They synthesize findings from prior studies, extract comparative advantages and limitations, and present multiple comparative summary tables (Tables 5–15) that collate algorithms, advantages/limitations, and reported experimental summary results from the cited literature. The paper does not report a formal systematic-search protocol (databases, search strings, inclusion/exclusion criteria, or PRISMA flow), nor does it perform original computational experiments; rather it compiles and discusses published methods and empirical results from existing studies to highlight trends, open challenges, and opportunities for quantum/quantum-inspired methods in finance.

key_findings: [supported] Portfolio optimization remains challenging because of dynamically changing market factors, changing constraints (liquidity, taxes, transaction costs), and high computational requirements.

[supported] Classical portfolio measures and methods (mean-variance, MAD, VaR, CVaR, minimax, lower partial moments) have useful properties but also notable limitations (estimation error, sensitivity to distributional assumptions, non-convexity, computational issues) and require regularization in practice.

[supported] Regularization, sparsity constraints and robust formulations (L2 regularization, semi-definite relaxation, time penalization) are effective strategies to reduce estimation error and transaction costs in portfolio models.

[supported] Machine learning and AI techniques (SVM, neural networks, LSTM, CNN hybrids and graph-based models) are increasingly applied to portfolio selection and can capture temporal dependencies and inter-asset relations, often improving empirical performance versus simple baselines in cited studies.

[supported] Reinforcement learning (including DDPG, PPO, policy gradients, deep Q-learning variants and recurrent RL) is well suited for dynamic portfolio management and has been shown in multiple cited works to learn adaptive, variable-weight allocation strategies.

[supported] Evolutionary and swarm-intelligence methods (GA, PSO, ACO, multi-objective evolutionary algorithms such as NSGA-II/SPEA2/MOPSO) are widely used for portfolio optimization and, in many empirical comparisons cited, outperform some classical optimization heuristics on constrained and combinatorial instances.

[supported] Quantum-inspired metaheuristics (quantum-inspired GA, quantum-inspired tabu search (QTS/MOQTS), quantum-inspired PSO/ACO, QIFAPSO, QIAEA) have been reported in the literature to improve convergence behavior and exploration/exploitation trade-offs relative to some classical counterparts in benchmark experiments.

[supported] Hybrid approaches that combine classical heuristics, deep learning and quantum(-inspired) methods have been prototyped for portfolio tasks and trading-rule optimization; some of these hybrids show favorable empirical returns or hit rates in cited experiments.

[supported] Specific experimental reports cited in the review claim that D-Wave hybrid quantum annealing and tensor-network (quantum-inspired) algorithms can handle large portfolio optimization instances (the paper cites ~1272 fully-connected qubits) and that D-Wave runs were comparatively fast while tensor-network methods yielded higher-quality solutions at greater computational cost.

[supported] Quantum-inspired tabu-search based trading systems (QTS) and multi-objective extensions (MOQTS) were reported in cited studies to outperform Buy & Hold and several classical rules on some historical datasets (examples and tables are presented).

[speculative] Quantum computing (true quantum hardware) offers potential for exponential state-space representation (2^n amplitudes for n qubits) that could help solve combinatorial portfolio optimization problems more efficiently in principle.

[speculative] Quantum-inspired/metaheuristic hybrids and quantum computing approaches are a promising direction for portfolio optimization but require further validation across broader financial datasets, realistic constraints, and out-of-sample tests.

[speculative] Claims about quantum hardware energy costs in the review (asserting quantum machines require much more energy than classical computers) are presented as concerns but are not established definitively within the paper.

[supported] Empirical hybrid ML/RL architectures and graph-convolutional RL (e.g., DeepPocket, GPM, multi-agent DRL frameworks) are proposed to improve explainability and to exploit inter-relations between assets.

[supported] The review concludes that evolutionary optimization and quantum-inspired techniques currently look promising as practical approaches for constrained and combinatorial portfolio problems, but that robust, reproducible, and scalable solutions remain active research challenges.
results_summary: This review surveys classical, statistical, machine-learning, evolutionary, reinforcement-learning and quantum(-inspired) approaches for portfolio optimization. Classical methods (mean-variance, MAD, VaR/CVaR, minimax, LPM) are foundational but limited by distributional assumptions and estimation error; regularization and robust/sparse models help mitigate these issues. Machine learning (including deep and graph models) and reinforcement learning provide adaptive, data-driven allocation strategies and show improved empirical performance in cited studies. Evolutionary and swarm-intelligence algorithms are effective for combinatorial and constrained portfolio problems. Quantum-inspired metaheuristics and early hybrid quantum/hardware approaches (e.g., quantum annealing, VQE, tensor networks) are reported to improve convergence and tackle larger instances in some experiments, but the review frames true quantum advantage as promising rather than conclusively demonstrated and calls for further empirical validation.

Benchmark comparisons in the review (Table 13) show the quantum-inspired acromyrmex evolutionary algorithm (QIAEA) achieving 100% hit accuracy on several tested functions (e.g., functions 1, 5, 10, 12, 14 in that table) across the presented experimental setup. [supported]
quantum_advantage_detail: The review reports promising empirical results for quantum-inspired metaheuristics and hybrid quantum approaches (including quantum annealers and tensor-network methods) on specific portfolio instances, but it does not present conclusive, general-purpose demonstrations of provable quantum speedup or broad quantum advantage. The paper frames quantum/quantum-inspired methods as promising and empirically favorable in selected studies while noting practical uncertainties, energy and scalability concerns, and the need for further validation.
limitations: Mean-variance (Markowitz) approaches: cannot be employed for large-scale problems due to heavy covariance computation; assume normally distributed returns and perform poorly with non-normal/asymmetric distributions.
Mean-absolute deviation (MAD): penalizes both positive and negative deviations; may skip covariance information leading to calculation risks.
Minimax: sensitive to outliers; cannot be used when historical data is missing.
Lower Partial Moment (LPM): computation of portfolio risk is tedious; sensitive to outliers.
Value-at-Risk (VaR): simplistic and can be misleading; does not measure worst-case loss; discrete, non-convex and non-smooth; requires near-perfect data/knowledge and is prone to estimation errors.
Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR): handles extreme losses but does not indicate the maximum possible loss.
Many traditional techniques suffer from estimation error and require regularization.
Support Vector Machines (SVM): underperform when classes overlap or data are noisy; not ideal for very large datasets.
Neural networks / deep models: not self-explanatory (lack interpretability); no prescriptive rules for network architecture selection.
Recurrent models (e.g., LSTM): suffer from vanishing/exploding gradients; hard to implement.

Reinforcement learning (RL): not suitable for very simple problems or very small datasets; vulnerable to the curse of dimensionality; too much reinforcement signal can hurt learning; initial allocations can cause losses before learning converges; many RL formulations are computationally heavy and require current market state information.
Evolutionary/metaheuristic approaches: higher computational requirements; results can be non-explanatory and non-reproducible; parameter tuning is difficult.
Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO): lacks rigorous mathematical foundation; may converge prematurely; not naturally suited for discrete problems; sensitive to initialization.
Ant Colony Optimization (ACO): convergence time not guaranteed; probabilistic dynamics can change and slow adaptation when topology changes.
Multi-objective evolutionary algorithms (MOEAs): lack of reproducibility; difficult parameter tuning and control.
Bayesian approaches: no universal method to construct networks from data; training may not use all patterns; choosing priors is nontrivial.
GARCH-based approaches: sensitivity to data frequency.

Quantum and quantum-inspired methods: many unknowns remain; some quantum-inspired algorithms are not efficient as item quantities grow; some cannot handle multi-objective scenarios; lack of experimental evidence in portfolio contexts for several quantum-inspired variants.

Quantum hardware approaches: tradeoffs noted (e.g., D-Wave hybrid quantum annealing is very fast, tensor-network methods can be higher quality but much more computationally expensive); practical energy requirements and other resource costs remain concerns.
QTS (quantum-inspired Tabu Search): degrades with increasing number of items.
QIFAPSO (quantum-inspired firefly + PSO): no experimental findings reported in portfolio optimization.
QIAEA (quantum-inspired acromyrmex evolutionary algorithm): cannot be used for multiple-objective scenarios.
General practical constraints: dynamically changing market factors, regulatory/liquidity/transaction-cost constraints, and the need for high computational power to produce timely allocations.
